name: ความเครียดทางอารมณ์
preview_text: เหตุการณ์ตึงเครียดแบบเดียวกันนี้อาจทำให้คนหนึ่งถอนหายใจแน่นหน้าอก อีกคนหน้าแดงและตะโกน และหนึ่งในสามหมดแรงเกินกว่าจะลุกจากเตียงได้ TCM ไม่ถามว่า 'เครียดแค่ไหน...
categories: ["อารมณ์ ความวิตกกังวล และสุขภาพทางอารมณ์"]
synonyms: ["Emotional Stress Weakening Resistance", "Susceptibility to illness during stressful periods"]
conventional_description: In Western medicine, emotional stress is understood as the body's response to perceived demands or threats, involving the nervous, endocrine, and immune systems. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis triggers the release of cortisol and adrenaline, leading to physical symptoms such as muscle tension, headaches, digestive upset, and a racing heart. Psychological symptoms include anxiety, irritability, low mood, and difficulty concentrating. Diagnosis is typically based on self-reported symptoms and their impact on daily function, often using screening tools like the Perceived Stress Scale.
conventional_treatments: Conventional management usually combines psychological approaches with lifestyle modification and, when needed, medication. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), mindfulness-based stress reduction, and counseling are first-line talk therapies. Medications may include antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs) for chronic stress-related anxiety or depression, short-term anxiolytics for acute episodes, and beta-blockers for physical symptoms like palpitations. Sleep hygiene, exercise, and relaxation techniques are routinely recommended as supportive measures.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, emotional stress is understood through the lens of Qi movement and organ system balance. The seven emotions - anger, joy, worry, pensiveness, sadness, fear, and fright - each have a natural affinity with a specific organ: anger with the Liver, joy with the Heart, worry and pensiveness with the Spleen, sadness with the Lungs, and fear and fright with the Kidneys. When an emotion is felt intensely or persists for too long, it disrupts the normal flow of Qi in its related organ, creating a pattern of disharmony. This is why chronic frustration tends to knot Liver Qi, while excessive rumination weakens the Spleen.
The Liver is the organ most commonly involved in emotional stress because it governs the smooth flow of Qi throughout the entire body. When Liver Qi flows freely, emotions are regulated and the mind feels calm. But when stress, frustration, or suppressed anger block this flow, Qi stagnates - and that stagnation can then generate Heat, flare upward as Fire, or even obstruct Blood circulation over time.
This explains the progression from simple irritability and sighing to explosive anger, a bitter taste, and a red face, and eventually to fixed, stabbing sensations when stress has lasted for years.
Yet not all emotional stress is about excess. In some people, particularly those who worry excessively or overthink, the Spleen's ability to produce Qi and Blood becomes depleted. When Blood is insufficient to nourish the Heart, the spirit (Shén) loses its anchor, leading to anxiety, palpitations, poor sleep, and a pervasive sense of fragility.
This pattern is just as real as Liver stagnation, but it feels entirely different - more like a drained battery than a pressure cooker - and requires a fundamentally different treatment approach. TCM's strength lies in distinguishing these patterns so that treatment can be precisely targeted.
classical_quote: 「怒则气上，喜则气缓，悲则气消，恐则气下，寒则气收，炅则气泄，惊则气乱，劳则气耗，思则气结。」
classical_translation: "Anger causes Qi to rise, joy causes Qi to slow, grief causes Qi to dissipate, fear causes Qi to descend, cold causes Qi to contract, heat causes Qi to leak, fright causes Qi to become chaotic, overexertion causes Qi to be consumed, and pensiveness causes Qi to knot."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking what the emotional stress actually feels like and how it shows up in your daily life. The character of the stress - whether it feels like a knot of frustration, a simmering heat, or a dull heaviness - provides the first vital clues. They will also want to know what makes it better or worse, how it affects your sleep and appetite, and whether you tend toward anger, worry, or sadness. These details begin to point toward one pattern rather than another.
If the stress feels like a stuck, pent-up frustration with chest tightness and frequent sighing, the practitioner suspects Liver Qi Stagnation. They will check your tongue for a thin white coating and your pulse for a wiry, tense quality. The key question is whether the emotional pressure feels contained and constrained, like something that needs to be released, rather than something that has already boiled over.
When that constrained feeling has lasted a long time and now comes with a bitter taste, dry mouth, and a sharper edge of irritability, the picture shifts to Liver Qi Stagnation transforming into Heat. The tongue now shows a redder body with a yellow coating, and the pulse becomes rapid as well as wiry. This tells the practitioner that the stagnation has generated internal heat, and the approach must now include cooling as well as moving the Qi.
If the stress presents as explosive anger, a red face, dizziness, and a very bitter taste, the practitioner thinks of Liver Fire Blazing. The tongue is red with a thick yellow coating, and the pulse is wiry and forceful - a sign of intense heat flaring upward. This pattern is more acute and intense than simple stagnation or even stagnation with heat, and it demands a different strategy to clear the fire.
When the stress feels more like a draining worry, with fatigue, poor appetite, palpitations, and insomnia, the practitioner looks toward Heart and Spleen Deficiency. The tongue is pale and the pulse is thin and weak. This picture points to a depletion of the energy that sustains both clear thinking and sound sleep, and the questions will focus on how worry has affected your digestion and rest.
For a heavier, more sluggish form of stress with a greasy taste, hypochondriac discomfort, and a sensation of damp heat, the practitioner considers Liver and Gallbladder Damp-Heat. The tongue coating is yellow and greasy, and the pulse is slippery and rapid. This pattern often arises when emotional stress combines with rich or irregular eating, and the diagnosis must account for both factors.
Finally, if the emotional stress has been present for many years and now includes fixed, stabbing pains, the practitioner suspects Qi and Blood Stagnation. The tongue is dark or purplish with possible stasis spots, and the pulse is choppy or wiry. This indicates that the long-standing constraint has moved beyond Qi into the blood level, and the diagnostic signs reflect that deeper level of stagnation.

patterns.symptoms: ["Distension or bloating along the ribs and flanks", "Frequent sighing", "Irritability or short temper", "Chest tightness", "Feeling of a lump in the throat (plum pit sensation)", "Worsens with frustration or emotional upset"]

patterns.why_this_happens:
The Liver is responsible for keeping Qi moving smoothly throughout the body. When you hold in frustration, suppress your feelings, or feel stuck in a stressful situation, that flow gets blocked. Think of it like a traffic jam: the Qi backs up in the Liver channel, which runs through the ribcage and chest. This pressure creates the hallmark distension and tightness along the ribs, and since the stuck Qi cannot rise and descend freely, you feel the need to sigh deeply to force movement.
This trapped Qi also disrupts the Liver's role in regulating mood, so irritability and mood swings follow directly from the blockage. The chest tightness and that classic lump-in-the-throat sensation are physical signs of Qi pressing in places it should not be.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly dusky body with red or purplish sides and a thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), taut like a guitar string, most noticeable at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional frustration and suppressed anger are the direct cause of Liver Qi Stagnation, so they immediately worsen the blockage. Skipping meals deprives the Liver of nourishment, while greasy foods create dampness that further obstructs Qi. Gentle movement and talking through feelings both help Qi to flow again rather than stagnate, which is the core treatment principle. Fresh herbs and small regular meals support the Liver's function without overwhelming it.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat regular, warm meals and avoid skipping breakfast, which stresses the Liver. Favor mildly pungent and dispersing foods like fresh herbs (mint, basil, coriander), small amounts of fennel or cumin, and leafy greens. Limit greasy, fried, or rich foods that clog the Qi flow. Gentle daily movement - a walk, stretching, or yoga - helps the Liver release stagnant Qi. Journaling or talking through frustrations prevents pressure from building up.

patterns.why_this_happens: When stress and frustration linger unresolved, Liver Qi gets stuck. Over time, that pent-up energy generates Heat, which then flares upward, turning simple irritability into explosive anger. The Heat also disturbs the mind and dries body fluids, leading to restlessness, a bitter taste, and insomnia.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red body with redder sides, yellow coating. Pulse: Wiry and rapid (弦数 xián shuò), forceful at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: When Liver Qi is already stagnant and generating Heat, anything that adds more heat-like spicy food, alcohol, or hot weather-intensifies symptoms. Anger and frustration directly aggravate Liver stagnation, fueling the fire. Cooling foods and a calm environment help clear Heat and soothe the Liver, while gentle exercise and emotional expression allow Qi to move freely, preventing further buildup. Stress management and rest nourish Yin, which helps anchor rising Yang and calm the mind.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat cooling, light foods like cucumber, celery, watermelon, and chrysanthemum tea. Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which add heat. Gentle exercise such as walking, yoga, or tai chi helps move Qi and release tension. Practice deep breathing or meditation to calm the mind. Try not to suppress emotions; express frustration in healthy ways.

patterns.why_this_happens: When anger or frustration is intense and persistent, Liver Qi can transform into Fire that flares upward. This rising Fire disturbs the mind, producing intense irritability, a short temper, and a restless, agitated feeling. The heat also burns the body's fluids, leading to dry mouth, a bitter taste, and constipation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with redder sides, dry yellow coating, possible red prickles. Pulse: wiry and rapid, full and forceful especially at the left Guan (Liver) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Liver Fire is a pattern of excess heat that surges upward, so anything that adds heat-spicy food, alcohol, or emotional anger-intensifies it. Cooling foods and a calm environment directly counteract the heat, while gentle movement helps disperse the stagnant Qi that feeds the fire.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Favour cooling, light foods such as cucumber, celery, chrysanthemum tea, and mung beans. Avoid spicy, greasy, or fried dishes, and reduce alcohol and coffee. Gentle exercise like walking or yoga can help smooth Liver Qi, but avoid overexertion. Prioritize calming activities and avoid situations that trigger anger.

patterns.symptoms: ["Anxiety and feeling easily startled", "Palpitations or a racing heart", "Poor appetite with bloating after meals", "Fatigue that is not relieved by rest", "Pale, sallow complexion"]
patterns.worse_with: Excessive worry and overthinking, Skipping meals or eating on the go, Overwork or lack of rest, Cold, raw, or greasy foods, Irregular sleep
patterns.better_with: Rest and quiet time, Warm, nourishing meals, Gentle exercise or movement (walking, yoga, stretching), Consistent sleep routine, Managing worry and overthinking
patterns.why_this_happens: Excessive worry and pensiveness directly weaken the Spleen's ability to transform food into Qi and Blood. When the Spleen is weak, it fails to produce enough Blood to nourish the Heart, leaving the spirit unanchored. This results in the anxiety, palpitations, and fatigue that make emotional stress feel so physically draining.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale, tender body with teeth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: Fine, weak, and thready.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Worry and pensiveness directly weaken the Spleen’s ability to transform food into Qi and Blood, which is why emotional stress and poor digestion go hand in hand. When the Spleen is weak, it cannot produce enough Blood to anchor the Heart’s spirit, leading to anxiety, palpitations, and insomnia. Rest, nourishing meals, and gentle movement rebuild Spleen Qi and Heart Blood, while cold foods and overwork further deplete them, so avoiding these triggers is essential for recovery.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat regular, warm, cooked meals like soups and stews to support your Spleen. Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that are hard to digest. Prioritise rest and a consistent sleep schedule-your body rebuilds Qi and Blood during sleep. Gentle exercise like walking or tai chi can help circulate Qi without depleting energy. Most importantly, give yourself mental breaks from worry and overthinking; mindfulness or journaling can help settle the mind.

patterns.worse_with: Greasy or fried foods, Alcohol or coffee, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Damp, humid weather, Anger, frustration, or suppressed emotions
patterns.better_with: Cooling foods and drinks, Bitter greens and moderate watermelon, Gentle exercise or movement (walking, yoga, stretching), Staying well hydrated with plain water
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver is meant to keep Qi flowing smoothly, but when Dampness and Heat build up-often from a rich diet and emotional strain-they clog the Liver and Gallbladder like a sticky, hot fog. This stagnation creates a sensation of being bloated, heavy, and irritable, as the trapped Heat agitates the mind and the obstructed Qi makes every frustration feel more intense. The bitter taste, nausea, and right-sided rib discomfort are the body’s signals that the Liver and Gallbladder are overwhelmed by this Damp-Heat burden.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, redder at the sides, with a thick yellow greasy coating that can’t be scraped off. Pulse: wiry, slippery, and rapid-like a taut string that’s also rolling and quick.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy foods, alcohol, and hot spices directly introduce or generate Damp-Heat, which then clogs the Liver and Gallbladder, making Qi stagnate and Heat rise to disturb the mind. This is why such indulgences quickly worsen the irritability and heavy feeling. On the other hand, light, cooling foods and adequate water help the body flush out Dampness and cool the Heat, while gentle movement keeps Qi moving and prevents the stagnation that feeds emotional tension. Managing anger is equally crucial, because emotional frustration further knots the Liver Qi, trapping Damp-Heat even more.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Steer clear of greasy, fried, and sugary foods, as well as alcohol-they are the main fuels for Damp-Heat. Embrace lightly cooked vegetables, moderate amounts of cooling fruits like watermelon, and bitter greens like dandelion leaves. Gentle daily movement such as walking or stretching helps Qi flow and drains Dampness without overheating the body.

patterns.worse_with: Anger, frustration, or suppressed emotions, Cold environment or cold drinks, Sedentary lifestyle or prolonged sitting, Cold, raw, or greasy foods
patterns.better_with: Gentle exercise or movement (walking, yoga, stretching), Warmth (warm compresses, warm drinks), Deep breathing, meditation, or stress management, Foods that move Blood (hawthorn, turmeric)
patterns.why_this_happens: When emotional stress goes unrelieved for a long time, Qi stagnation becomes entrenched and eventually obstructs the flow of Blood. This creates a vicious cycle where emotional tension leads to physical pain, and the pain then deepens the emotional distress. The result is a pattern of fixed, stabbing sensations and a sense of oppression in the chest that feels both physical and emotional.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dark body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦) and choppy (涩), like a taut string with a rough, uneven flow.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress causes Qi to stagnate, and when Qi cannot move Blood, stasis sets in. Cold congeals Blood and makes stasis worse, while warmth and gentle movement help Blood flow smoothly. Deep breathing and meditation unwind the Liver Qi tension at the root of the problem. Foods that invigorate Blood, like hawthorn and turmeric, directly support the body's ability to clear stasis, while heavy or cold foods slow everything down.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Gentle daily movement-walking, stretching, or yoga-keeps Qi and Blood circulating. Eat warm, cooked foods and include blood-moving ingredients like black fungus, hawthorn, and a little turmeric. Avoid cold, raw foods and heavy greasy meals that can congeal Blood. Practice slow, deep breathing or meditation to unwind emotional knots before they turn into physical pain.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help with emotional stress?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture works by regulating the flow of Qi in the channels connected to the organs most affected by stress - primarily the Liver, Heart, and Spleen. Most people feel noticeably calmer and less reactive after just a few sessions. The effect is not simply relaxation during the treatment; it is a resetting of the nervous system that builds over time. For best results, weekly sessions are recommended for at least 4-6 weeks.

faqs.question: How is TCM different from seeing a therapist?
faqs.answer: TCM and talk therapy address emotional stress from complementary angles. Therapy works with thoughts, beliefs, and behavioral patterns. TCM works with the physical substrate - the Qi, Blood, and organ systems that shape how emotions are experienced in the body. Many people find that after TCM treatment, the same stressful triggers no longer hit as hard, making psychological work easier. The two approaches can be used together very effectively.

faqs.question: Will I need to take herbs forever?
faqs.answer: No. Herbal formulas for emotional stress are typically taken for a defined period - usually weeks to months - to correct the underlying pattern. Once the pattern resolves, the herbs are discontinued. Some people with long-standing constitutional tendencies may benefit from a maintenance formula taken at a lower dose or only during high-stress periods, but this is not the same as indefinite daily use.

faqs.question: I'm already on an antidepressant. Can I still try TCM?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases acupuncture and herbs can safely complement conventional medication. However, certain herbs have sedative properties and should be combined cautiously with medications that cause drowsiness. Always bring a complete list of your medications to your TCM practitioner, and do not stop or adjust your prescribed medication without consulting your doctor. See our Safety section for more details.

faqs.question: Does stress really cause physical symptoms in TCM?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. TCM sees no separation between mind and body. When Liver Qi stagnates, you may feel a lump in the throat, rib-side distension, or breast tenderness. When worry weakens the Spleen, you may experience bloating, loose stools, and fatigue. These physical signs are not 'all in your head' - they are direct manifestations of the emotional pattern, and they often improve as the underlying imbalance is treated.

faqs.question: What's the difference between Liver Qi Stagnation and Liver Fire?
faqs.answer: Liver Qi Stagnation feels like pent-up frustration - you may sigh a lot, feel a tightness in the chest, and have mood swings but not explosive anger. Liver Fire is what happens when that stagnation simmers for too long and turns into Heat: the irritability becomes intense and eruptive, with a bitter taste, red face, and a short fuse. The treatment for stagnation focuses on moving Qi; for Fire, the priority is clearing Heat while still moving the Qi.

faqs.question: How long until I see results?
faqs.answer: Many people notice a shift within 2-4 weeks of starting herbs and acupuncture - better sleep, less reactivity, a greater sense of calm. If the stress is rooted in a deficiency pattern, progress is more gradual, with the first signs often being improved energy and appetite before the emotional tone lifts. Consistency with treatment is key; missing sessions or herbs will slow the process.

research.title: Acupuncture for depression
research.description: This Cochrane systematic review assessed acupuncture versus usual care, sham acupuncture, and medication for major depressive disorder. It included 64 studies and found that acupuncture moderately reduces the severity of depression, with fewer side effects than antidepressant medication. The evidence for anxiety outcomes was less clear but suggested a positive trend.
research.periodical: Smith CA, Armour M, Lee MS, Wang LQ, Hay PJ. Acupuncture for depression. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018; Issue 3. Art. No.: CD004046.

research.title: Xiao Yao San for anxiety disorders: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials
research.description: This systematic review evaluated 18 RCTs of Xiao Yao San (Free and Easy Wanderer) for anxiety disorders. The meta-analysis showed that Xiao Yao San was more effective than placebo or conventional anxiolytics in reducing Hamilton Anxiety Scale scores, with a lower incidence of side effects. Study quality was generally moderate, with small sample sizes.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, Han M, Liu Z, et al. Chinese herbal medicine Xiao Yao San for anxiety disorders: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. Journal of Ethnopharmacology. 2020; 259: 112941.

research.title: Acupuncture for stress urinary incontinence: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: Although this trial focused on a physical condition, it included a secondary analysis of emotional stress and quality of life. The acupuncture group showed significant improvements in stress perception and emotional well-being compared to sham acupuncture, supporting the idea that acupuncture can modulate the body’s stress response.
research.periodical: Liu Z, Liu Y, Xu H, et al. Effect of electroacupuncture on urinary leakage among women with stress urinary incontinence: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2017; 317(24): 2493-2501.
